text: Same model, same size, trained two ways.
This one learned by trial and error, like everything we’ve done so far.
And this one just copied the worked answers of a much bigger model.
Wait. The copier wins? By that much?
On every test they tried. By the end, you’ll know why, and when copying isn’t enough.
Distillation versus RL. Episode one.
Think about learning to cook a hard dish. You can experiment in the kitchen.
Try something, taste it, adjust, try again. Hundreds of times.
Or you can borrow a great chef’s recipe notebook, and copy their steps, notes and all.
Copying sounds way faster.
It is. But you’ll only ever be as good as the notebook. In AI, experimenting is RL. Copying the notebook is called distillation.
Here’s the real difference. With RL, a whole attempt earns just one number.
So the model has to work out which part of the answer deserved it?
Exactly. With distillation, the student sees the teacher’s finished answer, every step included.
So every single word comes with a right answer: this is what the next word should be.
That’s a far richer signal. In practice, it just means fine-tuning on the teacher’s written-out answers.
That’s what DeepSeek did, with R1 as the teacher.
They curated about eight hundred thousand samples with it, around six hundred thousand of them with reasoning.
Then they fine-tuned six smaller open models on them.
Copying only. No reinforcement learning at all.
And then they did the fair test, right? Same model, both ways?
Yes. They took the same thirty-two billion parameter base model.
One copy got large-scale RL for over ten thousand steps. Here are its scores on four tests.
Now the copy that copied R1. Every bar goes up.
And by the most on the hardest tests: competition maths, and coding.
So RL is just... worse?
Why did trial and error lose here?
Pause, and have a guess.
C! It just needed more training. Give it longer and it catches up.
Tempting, but they trained it for over ten thousand steps. It’s B.
Remember how GRPO learns. It can only make good answers more likely if it samples some in the first place.
A smaller model, on a hard problem, tries six times. Zero. Zero. Zero, every time.
All the same score, so there’s nothing to learn.
Like a group where nobody ever gets a treat.
Right. Distillation skips that search. It just hands the student the good chain of reasoning.
Oh, so copying gives it something to aim at!
Eight hundred thousand examples sounds like a lot. Two 2025 papers asked: how few would do?
A paper called s1 used just one thousand carefully chosen examples.
Another, called LIMO, used eight hundred and seventeen. Both got strong maths results.
Eight hundred?! So Tiny only needs a thousand examples!
Careful. Both used thirty-two billion parameter models. A tiny model has much less knowledge to unlock.
And every example was filtered hard. A thousand random answers is not the same thing.
So which one should we use?
Often, both. Copy first to learn the habit of thinking, then experiment with GRPO to sharpen it on your exact task.
DeepSeek-R1 itself did that: a small copying stage first, then RL. And the student starts RL already getting some answers right.
One warning: students copy the teacher’s habits too. Including thinking for a long time.
Quick recap.
RL learns from one score. Distillation gets the right next word, every time.
On smaller models, copying R1 beat trial and error, by a lot.
And the best recipe is often: copy first, then experiment.
So let’s try it, on Tiny’s big sibling, Qwen, the real half-a-billion-parameter model.
We’ll show it about a thousand worked answers from a reasoning model’s notebook.
Long ones. Full of wait, let me check.
Hang on. If it copies everything... does it copy the skill? Or just the style? All the waits, and none of the checking?
That’s exactly what we’ll measure.
